strengths: Clear, practically important motivation: inference latency is a genuine bottleneck for TTA deployment, and the paper delivers a demonstrable ~100x real-time-factor speedup (RTF 0.013 vs 1.612 for GenAU) while remaining competitive on fidelity metrics.

Strong and well-organized empirical results: MeanAudio achieves the best single-step FAD/FD/CLAP among accelerated TTA systems (Table 1) with only 120M backbone parameters, and remains competitive in the multi-step regime (25 NFE), which is a meaningful efficiency-quality trade-off.

Thorough and well-designed ablations (Tables 2-4) that isolate each design choice: the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum, the flow field mix-up ratio (r=t), and the CFG scale. The ablation showing vanilla flow matching fails at 1 NFE (CLAP -0.007) is a convincing motivation for the curriculum.

Good reproducibility practices: the paper specifies architecture (N1=4, N2=8, hidden 448), sampling schedule (logit-normal, mu=0.4, sigma=1), guidance parameters (omega=0.3, kappa=0.9), training schedule, hardware, and commits to releasing code and weights.
The paper is clearly written and logically structured, with the method, training algorithm (Algorithm 1), and inference procedure (Algorithm 2) presented cleanly.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to the framing. The MeanFlow objective (Eq. 2) and the integration of classifier-free guidance into the training target are directly adapted from Geng et al. (2025); the genuinely new component is the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow field mix-up, which is essentially a two-stage training recipe. The 'first to apply MeanFlow to TTA' claim is an application-level contribution rather than a methodological advance.

Evaluation is narrow. All quantitative results are on a single test set (AudioCaps, 957 clips, one randomly chosen caption per clip). There is no out-of-domain evaluation, no human/MOS listening test, and no statistical significance or variance reporting, despite the paper repeatedly claiming 'faithful' generation. For a TTA paper making quality claims, a subjective evaluation would materially strengthen the evidence.

Missing relevant baselines. FlashAudio (Liu et al., 2025), a rectified-flow fast TTA model cited in the related work, is not compared against, even though it is one of the closest few-step competitors. The paper also does not compare against the original MeanFlow-style baselines for audio, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed curriculum versus the underlying MeanFlow objective.

Internal inconsistency in the results narrative. The paper states that quality improves as sampling steps increase, but MeanAudio's FAD is best at 2 NFE (1.53) and degrades at 5 NFE (1.67) and 25 NFE (1.74), and FD/IS/CLAP show non-monotonic behavior for several baselines as well. This undercuts the stated speed-fidelity trade-off claim and is not discussed.

The reported relative improvements ('FAD by 23.3%, FD by 22.2%, KL by 7.7%, IS by 6.8%, CLAP by 8.9%') are not tied to a clearly identified baseline; checking against Table 1, some figures match ConsistencyTTA while the FD figure does not match any listed single-step baseline, making the headline improvement claims difficult to verify.

The theoretical justification for the curriculum and the 75% mix-up ratio is intuitive rather than rigorous. There is no analysis of why mixed flow fields stabilize training, when the recipe would fail, or how sensitive it is to the pre-training/fine-tuning data split, beyond the empirical sweep in Table 3.

The claim of being 'state-of-the-art' is somewhat overstated for the multi-step setting, where TangoFlux achieves better IS (12.81 vs 11.14) and TangoFull-FT achieves better KL (1.24 vs 1.26); the paper itself hedges to 'competitive' in places, and this should be stated consistently.

Venue fit is somewhat tangential. While TTA has appeared at ACL, the paper's core contribution is an audio-generation systems/efficiency result with little connection to language processing beyond using FLAN-T5/CLAP as text encoders.

strengths: The paper presents the first application of MeanFlow to text-to-audio generation, combining a Flux-style latent transformer with mean flow objectives, integrated classifier-free guidance, and a two-stage training curriculum. The approach is technically sound and clearly motivated.

Empirical results are strong: MeanAudio achieves state-of-the-art single-step TTA performance with only 120M parameters and an RTF of 0.013, corresponding to roughly 100x speedup over diffusion-based baselines, while also delivering competitive or superior multi-step generation results.

The ablation studies are thorough and informative, systematically validating the proposed instantaneous-to-mean curriculum, the flow field mix-up ratio, and the integrated CFG scale. These ablations support the central design choices.

Reproducibility is well supported: the paper provides detailed architecture, hyperparameters, training schedule, hardware requirements, datasets, evaluation metrics, and promises open-source code and model weights.
The work has clear practical relevance, enabling fast, low-resource, real-time text-to-audio generation and making a strong case for efficient generative audio systems.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: the core objective is adapted from existing MeanFlow work, and the main contributions are the application to TTA, integrated CFG during training, and the training curriculum. These are useful but incremental adaptations rather than fundamentally new generative modeling ideas.

The paper lacks human evaluation (e.g., MOS or preference tests) to support claims of faithful and high-quality audio generation. Automated metrics such as FAD, FD, KL, IS, and CLAP are useful but do not fully capture perceptual fidelity or prompt faithfulness.

There is an inconsistency between the textual CFG formula and Algorithm 1: the text defines v_t^cfg = ω v_t + κ f_θ(x_t,t,t|C) + (1−ω−κ) f_θ(x_t,t,t|∅), while Algorithm 1 line 8 appears to swap the conditional and unconditional terms. The stated effective guidance scale ω′ = ω/(1−κ) is also not clearly derived from the formula, which harms clarity and reproducibility.

Evaluation is limited to the AudioCaps test set. Since Clotho and WavCaps are used during training, the paper does not demonstrate zero-shot generalization or cross-dataset robustness, which would better support broad TTA claims.

The final training configuration uses 75% standard flow matching (r=t) and only 25% mean flow objective, meaning the model is still dominated by vanilla flow matching during fine-tuning. The paper could better analyze why such a small fraction of mean flow samples is sufficient and whether the gains come primarily from MeanFlow or from other components.
Several recent accelerated TTA baselines cited in related work (e.g., SoundCTM, FlashAudio, Presto) are not included in the main comparison, so the empirical positioning is not fully comprehensive.

The paper does not report variance or confidence intervals for the metrics, making it difficult to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements. There is also no discussion of limitations, ethical considerations, or potential misuse of text-to-audio generation systems.

strengths: The problem is practically important and well-motivated: reducing the inference latency of text-to-audio (TTA) generation is a genuine bottleneck, and the paper targets it with a lightweight (120M-parameter) model that requires only consumer-grade GPUs (4x RTX 3090) to train.

The paper is generally clear and well organized: the preliminaries on conditional flow matching and mean flows are presented cleanly, the architecture (Flux-style MMDiT/DiT, ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, AdaLN conditioning) is described in reproducible detail, and Algorithms 1-2 specify training and inference.

The ablation suite (Tables 2-4) is informative on its own terms: the curriculum stages, the flow mix-up ratio r=t, and the CFG guidance scale are each varied with both single-step and 25-step metrics, and the CFG ablation (Table 4) is a sensible sanity check.
Data hygiene is handled thoughtfully: overlapping audio between training sources and the AudioCaps test split is filtered, and the training set is described with durations and sources.

The reported single-step numbers (e.g., FAD 1.77, CLAP 0.292 at 1 NFE) are competitive with other accelerated TTA models, and the model is small relative to baselines (>500M parameters), which is a real practical advantage if the numbers hold up.
weaknesses: Novelty is thin. MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025) is an existing method, integrating classifier-free guidance into the training target is also from Geng et al. (2025), and the backbone (Flux-style MMDiT+DiT, ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, AdaLN) is assembled from prior work. The only genuinely new element is a two-stage pretrain/finetune curriculum with a mix-up ratio, which amounts to standard pretraining followed by fine-tuning. The headline claim 'first study to apply MeanFlow in TTA' is a narrow modality-transfer first, not a conceptual contribution.

The central ingredient (mean flow) is undercut by the paper's own ablation. Table 3 shows that pure mean-flow fine-tuning (0% r=t) collapses (CLAP -0.090), and the best configuration uses 75% vanilla flow matching. There is no control that fine-tunes with 100% flow matching on the same data/compute, so it is not established that the mean-flow objective contributes anything beyond the flow-matching pretraining; the framing of 'MeanAudio' as a mean-flow method is therefore weaker than presented.

A key ablation is confounded. Table 2 compares MeanAudio_PT (trained on ALL four datasets, 96h) against MeanAudio (AudioCaps only, 116h). Data, objective, and compute differ simultaneously, so the claimed benefit of the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum cannot be attributed cleanly; a same-data, same-compute FM fine-tuning baseline is missing.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper calls itself 'self-contained, requiring no established teacher,' yet it depends on pretrained FLAN-T5, CLAP, a VAE, and a vocoder. The '100x speedup' is measured against 200-NFE diffusion systems, while against the comparable accelerated models the wall-clock gain is only ~1.3-1.8x (RTF 0.013 vs. 0.017/0.023); the abstract and Figure 1 lean on the more dramatic comparison. The abstract's 'smooth and coherent transitions across successive synthesis steps' is never operationalized or measured.

Evaluation is too narrow and lacks statistical grounding. There is a single test set (957 AudioCaps clips), one randomly sampled caption per clip (the other four captions are discarded, introducing sampling variance), no multiple seeds, no confidence intervals or significance tests, and no human listening test despite repeated 'faithful'/'quality' claims. Small FD/FAD/CLAP gaps (e.g., 1.77 vs. 2.16 FAD) are treated as decisive without any indication of variance.

The reported relative improvements are not traceable. The text claims 'improves FD by 22.2%,' but the arithmetic against ConsistencyTTA's single-step FD (22.16 -> 15.40) is ~30%, and it is unclear which baseline each percentage refers to; similarly, Figure 1 lists AudioLCM at 150M and TangoFlux at 515M while Table 1 lists 160M and 516M. The symbol dagger is overloaded in Table 1 (baseline marker and parameter-count footnote), which makes the table harder to trust.

Reproducibility is incomplete for review. The 'Project - Code -' placeholders are empty, no checkpoints or code are provided in the submission, the IS classifier and KL computation are only partially specified, and baseline RTFs depend heavily on implementation-level optimization, so the speed comparison is not apples-to-apples.

Notational and clarity problems exist: Algorithm 1 alternates between f_theta(x_t, r, t) and f_theta(x_t, t, t, empty-set) signatures, and the JVP/stop-gradient handling in Eqs. 1-2 and the u_tgt derivation are easy to misread. Recent accelerated TTA systems that are cited (FlashAudio, Presto, Stable-Audio-Small, SoundCTM) are not compared experimentally, leaving the positioning of the contribution unclear.

Relevance to computational linguistics is limited: the language component is a frozen FLAN-T5/CLAP encoder, and the contribution is an audio-generation systems/engineering result rather than a finding about language processing.

strengths: The paper presents the first application of Mean Flows to text-to-audio generation, enabling high-quality single-step (1-NFE) synthesis and substantially reducing inference cost compared with diffusion-based TTA systems.
The proposed architecture is well motivated: dual text encoders (FLAN-T5 and CLAP), ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, and SwiGLU are ablated, showing clear benefits for fidelity, alignment, and stability.
Integrated classifier-free guidance into the training target avoids extra forward passes at inference, and the ablation on guidance scale supports the design choice.

The instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow-field mix-up is a useful training strategy; ablations on curriculum and mix-up ratio demonstrate improved single-step and multi-step generation performance.
The empirical study is broad: objective results on AudioCaps and MusicCaps, human subjective evaluation, scaling experiments, and dataset statistics support the main claims.

The model is efficient in practice: 120M parameters, trained on four RTX 3090 GPUs, with a reported RTF of 0.013 and promised code/weight release, making the work relevant for practical TTA deployment.
weaknesses: The classifier-free guidance formulation is internally inconsistent: Eq. (3) and Algorithm 1 swap the conditional/unconditional terms, and the stated effective guidance scale ω/(1-κ) does not follow from the displayed expression. This harms reproducibility and theoretical clarity.

The speed comparison may be insufficiently controlled: RTF values for baselines may come from different hardware or implementations, so the claimed 100x speedup over GenAU is not fully established as an apples-to-apples comparison.

Methodological novelty is limited: Mean Flows already exists, and the paper mainly adapts it to TTA with architectural and training-curriculum improvements rather than introducing a fundamentally new generative framework.

Important recent fast TTA methods (e.g., FlashAudio, SoundCTM, Presto) are discussed but not fully compared in the main results, and some closed-source baselines outperform MeanAudio on certain objective metrics, so the state-of-the-art claim needs qualification.

The evaluation uses only one randomly selected caption per AudioCaps test clip and does not report confidence intervals or significance tests; the human evaluation involves 10 raters and limited samples per model, with no significance testing.

Several implementation details remain underspecified or deferred to appendices (e.g., exact JVP computation, weak-label preprocessing), and the code/demo links are blank in the submitted manuscript, limiting immediate reproducibility.

The limitations are acknowledged but non-trivial: 10-second cropped audio, inability to generate intelligible speech, and noisy public training data constrain the practical scope and impact of the model.

strengths: Presents the first application of MeanFlows to text-to-audio generation, enabling high-quality 1-NFE synthesis and a strong efficiency/quality trade-off.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on AudioCaps and MusicCaps with objective metrics, subjective human ratings, and extensive ablations (curriculum, flow mix-up, architecture, CFG scale, data/model scaling).
Achieves a real-time factor of 0.013 on an RTX 3090 with a compact 120M-parameter model, reporting a 100x speedup over GenAU and strong single-step generation results.

Architectural and training contributions are well motivated and validated: dual text encoders (FLAN-T5 + CLAP), ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, integrated CFG training, and an instantaneous-to-mean curriculum.
Ablations provide useful best practices for MeanFlow-based audio generation, including the importance of pre-training, 75% flow mix-up ratio, and guidance scale around 3.
Human evaluation aligns with objective results and supports the claimed gains in overall quality and prompt relevance.
The paper is clear, well structured, and discusses limitations transparently.
weaknesses: Code and demo links are absent in the submitted manuscript, so reproducibility currently depends on the promised future release.

Several notation/typographical inconsistencies appear: the CFG mixing equation and effective guidance scale are confusingly presented, and the objective/subjective evaluation descriptions are swapped in Section 4.2.

The headline 100x speedup is primarily against GenAU, which uses 200 NFEs and 1250M parameters; comparisons with similarly sized accelerated models (e.g., AudioLCM at 160M and 1 NFE with RTF 0.023) show much smaller speed gains.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim needs qualification: MeanAudio's IS and CLAP scores are slightly below GenAU's 200-step results, so the advantage is mainly in single-step generation and efficiency rather than across all metrics.
Objective metrics lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests; the human evaluation does not report inter-annotator agreement.
The method is evaluated only on 10-second audio clips and public datasets, and does not handle speech or long-form audio, limiting broader applicability.
The core technical novelty is largely an adaptation of MeanFlows with architectural refinements, which may be viewed as incremental relative to the original MeanFlow contribution.

strengths: Presents a fast text-to-audio generation system with 1-NFE inference, a compact 120M-parameter model, and strong reported objective results (e.g., AudioCaps single-step FD 14.30, IS 10.02, CLAP 0.290) with RTF 0.013 on an RTX 3090.

Introduces a two-stage instantaneous-to-mean training curriculum and flow-field mix-up, and ablations in Tables 3 and 4 show these choices improve single-step generation and training stability over standard flow matching.
Evaluates both objective metrics and human ratings, including multi-step generation and text-to-music transfer, which strengthens the empirical picture relative to a purely single-benchmark study.

The dual text encoder design (FLAN-T5 + CLAP) is ablated, and the reported CLAP improvement (0.285 vs. 0.270 without CLAP) provides some evidence that the added global conditioning is useful for prompt adherence.
weaknesses: The classifier-free guidance formulation is internally inconsistent and unclear. Equation 3 places the conditional term under κ and the unconditional term under (1−ω−κ), while Algorithm 1 line 8 assigns κ to the unconditional term and (1−ω−κ) to the conditional term. With ω=0.3 and κ=0.9, the unconditional coefficient becomes negative, and the stated effective guidance scale ω/(1−κ)=3 is not derived or reconciled with standard CFG. The method also uses fθ(x_t,t,t|·) in the guidance target rather than fθ(x_t,r,t|·) used in training, making the central “integrated CFG” mechanism hard to reproduce or verify.

The architecture ablation in Table 5 does not support the claimed benefit of every component. The full model has higher FD (16.13) than the w/o RoPE variant (15.87) and lower IS (9.62) than both w/o CLAP (9.80) and w/o RoPE (9.83); the paper discusses only the CLAP and alignment metrics while ignoring these contradictory results.

The subjective evaluation is very small (10 raters, 10 samples), lacks inter-rater agreement or significance testing, and randomly selects only one of five captions per AudioCaps test clip, so the human-evaluation conclusions are weakly supported.

Reproducibility is limited: the code and demo links in the footnote are blank, model weights are not available, and several important details are underspecified, including how the CFG scale is varied in Table 6 if CFG is integrated into training, how AudioSet/VGGSound captions are generated, and exact architectural definitions for MMDiT/DiT variants.

The comparison setup is not fully apples-to-apples: MeanAudio is trained on 2.8M weakly labeled audio-text pairs while baseline models may use different training data, and the AudioCaps test set is small (957 clips). No statistical significance tests are reported for objective metrics, making the broad SOTA claim fragile.

The paper is primarily an audio/speech generation paper and may be peripheral to ACL’s core NLP scope; the contribution is also largely an adaptation of existing MeanFlow and Flux-style components, so the novelty is more engineering-oriented than methodological.

Clarity and consistency issues remain: notation changes between fθ(t,x_t), fθ(x_t,r,t), and fθ(x_t,t,t); variants such as MeanAudio-S-AC, MeanAudio-S-Full, MeanAudio-L-Full, and FluxAudio are used before being defined; and the “100x speedup” claim corresponds to roughly 124x by the reported RTFs.
